closing: AI-drafted question. No expert wrote or checked it. Answer in a few sentences, or say the question is badly put.

rows.title: About the extension strands: The Nature of Schooling and The Languages of Being Human
rows.description:
What these strands are for. They add two subjects to the Interdisciplinary model: how societies pass knowledge on, with schools as one arrangement among several, and how languages carry, change and compare ideas. They reuse the shared concepts of the first four strands (Teaching, Scaffolding, Institutions, Communication, Representation and others) and put them at the centre of a part. They have no counterpart in Bio-Core.

Held fixed with the other strands: the format (four grade bands, performance indicators, concepts tagged to parts, a 'does not carry over' note on each concept) and the drafting method (AI-drafted, then reviewed). Varies: the two subjects, and the use of four thinking tools (Tinbergen's questions, causal maps, payoff tables, analogy maps) at every band.

What it can say: how these concepts could be taught across the grade bands and where the comparisons break. What it cannot say: that this is the right way to teach either subject, that students learn from it, or how any named community learns or speaks. No class has used it and no person with expert knowledge has reviewed it.

Disclosures. The lab drafted everything with AI help. Two further AI reviews, which found and fixed errors, are the only checks so far. Sources were read from abstracts, publisher descriptions or catalogue entries, and only a few were read in full. The parts are drafts and stay out of the comparison views until a reviewer accepts them.

AI-drafted statement. No expert has checked it. If it misdescribes the strands, say so.

rows.title: Aim and theory: Education as a Changing System
rows.description: The part asks where evolutionary accounts of teaching and transmission have been applied to schools, and where critics say they leave out justice, care, power and who decides. Is that a fair account of the debate? Which writers on each side should a 9-12 student meet?

rows.title: Boundary: Educational Purpose
rows.description: The entry names seven levels (the learner, the family, the community, the school, the nation, the world and future generations) and three aims that compete (equal citizenship, skills for work, and sorting people for social position). Does that match how education researchers describe purposes? What is missing or put badly?

rows.title: Boundary: Schooling
rows.description: The entry says schools are several thousand years old and schooling for nearly every child is recent. Is that stated accurately? Does the 'does not carry over' note keep schooling from becoming the standard that other ways of learning are measured against?

rows.title: Boundary: Curriculum
rows.description: The entry separates the written, the taught and the learned curriculum and adds the hidden curriculum. One domain meaning borrows the word for the order of training examples in machine learning. Is that a helpful false friend for students, or a distraction?

rows.title: Boundary: Why Societies Build Schools
rows.description: One indicator asks students to describe how the choice of language of instruction helps some learners and makes learning harder for others. Does the part treat that choice fairly, including the history of schooling used to move children away from family languages and the wish of some communities to have their own languages taught?

rows.title: Order of steps: Many Places to Learn, Many Ways to Teach
rows.anchor: Many Places to Learn, Many Ways to Teach
rows.description: This part is stated to follow People Who Show Us How and to lead into Why Societies Build Schools. Is that the right order? Which indicator is too hard or too easy for 3-5?

rows.title: Sources: Why Societies Build Schools
rows.description: Six sources are attached, all read from abstracts, publisher descriptions or catalogue entries. Which central works are missing, especially from outside Europe and North America and from Indigenous and critical traditions? Which attached source would you drop?

rows.title: How progress shows: People Who Show Us How
rows.description: What would a K-2 child say that shows they see that people learn without a teacher? What would show they think learning happens only at school?

rows.title: Aim and theory: What Can We Conclude From Differences Between Languages
rows.anchor: What Can We Conclude From Differences Between Languages
rows.description: The part separates a weaker and a stronger version of the claim that language shapes thought, and says the strong version mostly fails when tested. Is that a fair statement of the evidence? Is the part pitched right for 9-12?

rows.title: Boundary: One Word, Two Meanings
rows.description: The entry treats a word that covers two meanings as a pattern in how a language packages meanings, and says it does not show that speakers link the two ideas. Is that the right caution? What would a lexical typologist change?

rows.title: Boundary: Language Family
rows.description: The entry says a family tree of languages hides borrowing and that languages in one family are not fully independent examples. Is that stated correctly? Is the comparison of a tree with a network, used in the 6-8 part, accurate?

rows.title: Boundary: Language
rows.description: The entry sets human language beside animal call systems, programming languages and language models, and says whether language models understand is debated. Are those comparisons fair? Is anything stated as settled that is not?

rows.title: Boundary: Languages Have Families and Neighbours
rows.description: The part gives four reasons two languages can have a similar word: a common ancestor, borrowing, imitation of a sound or baby talk, and chance. Are these the right four for 6-8? What would a historical linguist add or change?

rows.title: Boundary: Translation
rows.description: The entry says a draft translation by software or an AI helper needs review by a speaker of both languages. The 9-12 part uses a translation of a key idea such as evolution or agency as a case. Do you agree with that standard, and is the example a good one? Speakers of any language the translation touches are especially welcome.

rows.title: Order of steps: Words Travel and Change
rows.description: This part is stated to follow Many Ways to Say It and to lead into Languages Have Families and Neighbours. Is the message-chain exercise before borrowing the right order? What does a whispered-message game exaggerate?

rows.title: Sources: Languages Have Families and Neighbours
rows.description: Eight sources are attached, mostly read from abstracts and mostly by researchers based in Europe and North America. Which works on languages outside Europe, including South Asia and Africa, should be added? Which attached source would you drop?

rows.title: How progress shows: Many Ways to Say It
rows.description: What would a K-2 child say that shows they see that a word works because a group shares the habit of using it? What would show they think one language is the original and the others are copies?

rows.title: Boundary: payoff tables in the two new strands
rows.description: Four payoff tables sit in the two strands: a choice of trade language (6-8) and a choice of home language (9-12) in the language strand, and a choice of language for lessons (6-8) and a division of teaching (9-12) in the schooling strand. Each says whose choice it is and lists what the table leaves out. Do any of them risk presenting language loss or a school language policy as inevitable? What else should the 'left out' lists name?

rows.title: How progress shows: analogy maps and causal maps in the two new strands
rows.description: The analogy maps end in a break column and the causal maps mark who or what decides each arrow. Pick one map from each strand. Do the break columns name the main differences? Is the wording right for the band?
